title: Provide nutrition to plants and landscapes

lessons.title: What plants need to grow
lessons.html:
Plant food

Plants make sugars from sunlight, water and air. But they also need minerals (nutrients) from the soil to build leaves, roots and flowers. If a nutrient is missing, the plant shows signs of hunger.

The big three: N, P, K

NutrientMain jobSigns of shortage
Nitrogen (N)Green leaves and growthPale yellow older leaves, slow growth
Phosphorus (P)Roots, flowers, seedsPoor roots, purple tinge on leaves
Potassium (K)Strength, flowers, fruit, disease resistanceBrown, burnt leaf edges

Plants also need calcium, magnesium and sulphur, and small amounts of trace elements such as iron, zinc and boron. Yellow young leaves with green veins often mean iron shortage, common in alkaline soil.

Reading a fertiliser bag

In South Africa fertiliser bags show three numbers, such as 2:3:2 (22). The first three numbers are the ratio of N:P:K. The number in brackets is the total percentage of those nutrients in the bag. So 2:3:2 has more phosphorus, which is good for planting and root growth. A lawn fertiliser like LAN (limestone ammonium nitrate) is mainly nitrogen for green growth.

Organic and inorganic

  • Organic – compost, kraal manure, chicken manure, bone meal. Releases food slowly and improves the soil.
  • Inorganic (chemical) – granules or water-soluble powders. Fast acting and exact, but can burn plants if overused.

Soil testing by a laboratory tells your supervisor what the soil really needs, including the pH (acid or alkaline).

lessons.title: Applying fertiliser correctly
lessons.html:
Before you apply

  1. Get instructions: which product, how much per square metre or per plant, and where.
  2. Read the label. Follow its rates and safety advice.
  3. Check the soil is moist. Fertiliser on dry soil can burn roots.
  4. Wear gloves, and a dust mask for powders.

Methods

  • Broadcasting – spreading granules evenly over a lawn or bed by hand or with a spreader. Walk in straight lines, half the amount one way and half across, so there are no stripes.
  • Side dressing – placing fertiliser in a ring around a plant, away from the stem, under the outer leaves (drip line).
  • Liquid feeding – mixing soluble fertiliser with water and watering it on, or through the irrigation.
  • Mixing into soil – adding compost and planting fertiliser to the planting hole.

Measuring

If the instruction is 50 g per square metre and the bed is 4 m by 2 m (8 m²), you need 8 × 50 g = 400 g. Weigh it or use a marked cup. Never guess.

After applying

  • Water it in well, unless the label says otherwise. This moves food to the roots and stops burning.
  • Sweep fertiliser off paths and paving; it stains and washes into drains and rivers.
  • Record the date, product, amount and area.

Do not

  • Do not put fertiliser against stems or leaves.
  • Do not use more than the instruction; too much burns plants and pollutes water.
  • Do not apply before heavy rain.
  • Do not store fertiliser near food, fuel or in damp places.

Key points

  • N is for leaves, P for roots and flowers, K for strength and fruit.
  • A bag marked 2:3:2 (22) gives the N:P:K ratio and the total nutrient percentage.
  • Measure the right amount; never guess.
  • Apply to moist soil, keep it off stems and water it in.
  • Sweep up spills and record what you applied.
